prize_parts.citation: for establishing biomolecular phase separation as a physical-chemical principle of intracellular organization

statement.case_for: Biomolecular condensates changed how chemists and biologists describe the interior of the cell. Hyman and Brangwynne showed that P granules and nucleoli behave as liquid droplets, and Rosen showed that multivalent weak interactions are sufficient to reconstitute demixing in vitro. The concept is thermodynamic: saturation concentrations, phase diagrams, tunable material properties. It is a general principle of molecular organisation that links self-assembly, soft matter and cell biology, and it now informs disease-linked aggregation (including lipid- and protein-driven assemblies related to amyloid) and the design of synthetic compartments. Of the shortlisted work it is the clearest new concept of how matter organises itself in living systems, and physical chemistry of life is otherwise thinly represented on this shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and generality. The field is still debating how widely liquid-liquid phase separation, as opposed to other assemblies, operates under physiological conditions, and some in-cell claims have been challenged on methodological grounds. Credit is also spread: Pappu and Mittag (sequence grammar, stickers-and-spacers), and others, are left out of a three-person prize. Several colleagues with strong rankings, notably for base editing and degraders, point to work whose consequences are already tangible and whose chemistry is more clearly defined, so a few more years of consolidation could be argued for condensates.

responses.point: Base editing (B061) is a clear chemical principle with very large generative potential, early clinical use and good timing, and the 2020 Cas9 prize covers only the nuclease.
responses.response: I agree the principle is clean and the replication is strong, and I would not object to it. But the invention is an engineering of a known enzymatic reaction onto a programmable scaffold, and the 2020 prize is close enough that the committee may be seen as rewarding the same ecosystem twice. The attribution is also uncomfortable, since the decisive first authors are trainees and the Kondo/Nishida parallel work is left out. I rank it below condensates on conceptual novelty but would accept it as an alternative; I do not think my disagreement is about quality.

responses.point: Base editing converts a defined deaminase reaction into a general tool for single-nucleotide correction, is mechanistically clear, and is already used preclinically and clinically.
responses.response: I accept the mechanistic clarity and the clinical relevance. My qualification is that a prize for a tool, however good, differs from one for a new concept of how molecules organise; I would weigh the latter higher when the tool follows from a previously recognised platform. I would like to hear how you would settle the Liu-alone, Liu-Komor-Gaudelli and Kondo/Nishida question, because that determines whether the proposal is actually awardable.

responses.point: Condensates are a major conceptual change, but rapid expansion, contested physiological relevance and spread credit make recognition less secure than for degraders or genetic code expansion.
responses.response: This is a fair challenge and the part I take most seriously. In my own area I see how easily a phase diagram measured in vitro is over-read as proof of liquid behaviour in a cell, so I share your caution on contested claims. I would say, though, that the debate concerns the extent of the phenomenon, not the existence of demixing driven by multivalency, which is reproduced across many labs. The Hyman/Brangwynne/Rosen trio rests on the demonstrations that are least disputed, and Pappu and Mittag's theory is a later layer.

responses.point: Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics (B037) is a clean two-person attribution with four decades of validation, and a computational prize has precedent.
responses.response: The attribution and maturity are as good as any on the list, and as a physical chemist I value the method's descendants in interfaces and liquids. My concern is only that the list is competitive: B037 has a single first-place vote and almost no other support in the opening, so I doubt it can reach five votes. I would be glad to see it advance if colleagues argue that computation should be represented this year.

responses.point: Long-range electron transfer through proteins (B055) shows tunnelling through protein matrix with Marcus-type dependences, with decades of confirmation and a clear Gray-Winkler attribution.
responses.response: I find the physical content compelling and the attribution clean. Your own caveat that Marcus theory was recognised in 1992 matters to me: the experimental program is the more distinctive part, but the committee would need to explain what the prize adds. I would not rank it above condensates for breadth, and it has little support from other members so far, but I would keep it in view if consolidation becomes necessary.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the debate over physiological liquid-liquid phase separation to be settled enough for a prize now.
Whether Pappu and Mittag should be included in place of Rosen, or whether a three-person cut of the field is defensible at all.
Whether PROTACs and molecular glues can be recognised cleanly in three names, which decides if B028 is a better consensus candidate than B015.
Whether base editing follows too closely on the 2020 prize.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict is apparent from my profile: I have no personal or institutional tie to Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu or Mittag. My research on lipid-protein co-assembly and amyloid is scientifically adjacent to condensates, and I share Lund affiliation with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, which I flag for transparency only.
